title: Healthy Weight: Understanding BMI and Weight Management
content:
Body weight exists on a spectrum, and health is not determined by weight alone. However, both excess weight (overweight and obesity) and being underweight carry health risks, and evidence-based weight management can reduce those risks.

Body mass index (BMI) is a commonly used screening tool calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared (kg/m²). Standard adult BMI categories: Underweight — below 18.5; Healthy weight — 18.5–24.9; Overweight — 25–29.9; Obese — 30 and above. BMI is a population-level tool, not a precise individual health measure — it does not distinguish between fat mass and muscle mass, and its predictive value varies across ethnicities. For people of South Asian, East Asian, and some other ethnicities, cardiometabolic risk is elevated at lower BMI thresholds than those listed above.

Waist circumference is an additional measure. Excess abdominal (visceral) fat is particularly associated with cardiovascular and metabolic risk. General risk thresholds: above 88 cm (35 inches) for women, above 102 cm (40 inches) for men.

For those who are overweight or obese, even a modest weight loss of 5–10 percent of body weight is associated with meaningful improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol.

Evidence-supported approaches to weight management:

A sustained calorie deficit — consuming fewer calories than expended — drives weight loss. There is no single correct diet for everyone; the best diet is one that provides adequate nutrition and can be maintained long-term. Mediterranean-style and low-glycaemic-index eating patterns have strong evidence bases.

Physical activity supports weight loss and, more strongly, weight maintenance after loss. Resistance training helps preserve muscle mass during calorie restriction.

Behavioural strategies — self-monitoring of food intake and weight, setting specific goals, and addressing emotional eating — improve long-term outcomes.

Healthcare provider guidance is important for people with obesity-related health conditions. Medications and surgical options exist for people with significant obesity where lifestyle modification has been insufficient.

Weight loss should never be pursued through severely restrictive diets, skipping meals habitually, or other approaches that risk nutritional deficiency. If you have concerns about your weight, a registered dietitian and your primary care provider are the appropriate resources.
source: Original — based on CDC Healthy Weight guidance and NIH NIDDK weight management resources (public domain)
